The Smart Manufacturing Delivery RET (RoviSys Execution Template) is our project delivery flow based on our Dx procedures.  T his 
template outlines how each of the procedures flow together to define how we execute a comprehensive project within our "Agile for 
Manufacturing" mindset.  This mindset enables the continuous refinement of project scope throughout the lifecycle of a 
digitalization initiative. It bridges the gaps between purely agile and purely waterfall execution methodologies, addressing key 
challenges of both approaches.
Challenges with pure agile execution:
Lack of overall project goals and clear scope boundaries○

In many cases, a customer may be unfamiliar with the capabilities provided by an MES or MOM 
application, and there may be confusion as to the scope of the initiative as a result.  Even customers 
familiar with the digitalization of operations management functions may lack a deep understanding of 
capabilities provided by the different layers in the ISA -95 model, considering such systems as ERP,

as part of a digitalized ISA -95 compliant solution stack, focusing particularly on Level 3 capabilities most 
often provided by Layer 3 applications.  
Current Process State Definition:
This effort helps to baseline the current state of the facility or facilities under the scope of the 
assessment.  This exercise gives RoviSys background concerning current shop floor activities and system -
level processes that will help to frame the rest of the assessment effort.  
Stakeholder Group Interview Process:
During this activity, RoviSys learns more from key personnel in the enterprise about the processes and 
activities observed during current state process definition.  Probing questions are asked that allows 
RoviSys to draw conclusions concerning what processes work well and what processes could be 
enhanced by a greater degree of digitalization.  
Perceived Benefit: (Next Steps Value Identification)
During this activity, the perceived benefit of pursuing a next step is documented and a justification 
formulated.  While a formal ROI analysis is not typically conducted at this stage, distillment of the 
benefits of moving forward will aid the customer in justifying a larger initiative and provide the customer 
a more specific focus for constrained budgets and resources.  For example, RoviSys may recommend a

these productized services offerings.

various stakeholders who will need to participate in current process state explanations, interviews, and

to support a digitalization initiative, identifying aspects that may need to be bolstered as part of the

maintenance concerns.  This will help to ensure no key piece of legacy functionality is overlooked and 
that ultimately a holistic architecture is created detailing which applications will be replaced and which 
will be integrated into the future solution.

Current Process State Definition
This effort helps to baseline the current state of the facility or facilities under the scope of the 
assessment.  This exercise gives RoviSys background concerning current shop floor activities and system -
level processes that will help to frame the rest of the assessment effort, including specific topics to 
discuss and questions to ask during stakeholder interviews.  
The following are typical means by which RoviSys gathers current process state information:
Documentation Review:
The customer may possess legacy documentation that can be reviewed in an offline manner.  This 
includes user manuals, SOPs, piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs), swimlane diagrams, process 
flows, etc.  Early in the assessment initiative RoviSys should formulate an ask for such documentation.  
However, care must be taken not to spend too much time reviewing legacy documentation that may be 
incorrect or may be cumbersome / confusing when a more direct means of obtaining the same 
information (site tours, stakeholder reviews, etc.) may be more efficient.  
Conference Room Overview:
During this session, the customer walks RoviSys through the manufacturing process, including key user 
and/or system touchpoints.  It can be advantageous to discuss how the site / enterprise operates in a 
conference room setting prior to the site tour as it is easier to communicate and ask questions in a 
meeting setting than on the floor with noise and other distractions.  This discussion provides a baseline 
for the site tour that allows more useful details to be gathered during the tour.  
Site Tour:
The primary goal of a site tour is not to understand the customer's manufacturing and supporting 
business processes, as this information can be more easily obtained offline.  Rather, the site tour helps 
to establish perspective that may weigh into the subsequent business intentions and business process 
scenarios.  Some examples include the following:
The speed at which production moves on the shop floor-
Locations at which manual operations occur or areas where key data may be captured in an 
automated manner-
The size and scale of the facility, which may necessitate or eliminate certain solution options (such 
as mobile devices, vision systems, etc.)-
The scope of an operator's tasks-
Opportunities for overhead visualizations, stack lights, paging, and other notification conduits-
Locations where whiteboards or bulletin boards may exist to capture or convey information that 
could be replaced with a digital system-
Usage of paper work instructions-
Methods of identifying raw materials, WIP product, and finished goods (labels, barcodes, etc.)-
The site tour can also help to highlight concerns that can be discussed during the stakeholder interview 
process, including the following examples:(Published) MES RIS 101.9 -Current Process State Definition

Large buildups of staged WIP product between stations-
Lines / machines not running-
Alarms-
Large amounts of scrap or suspect product-
Paper -based operations (tickets, travelers, labels, etc.) -
Inefficient work processes (Operator has to walk large distances to complete tasks, perform 
multiple disconnected operations in sequence, etc.)-
Lastly, the site tour can permit access to speak to operators, supervisors, quality techs, etc. first hand to 
gain insights concerning how these individuals perform their daily work, concerns, or ideas they may 
have for improvement.  The tour will not allow every scenario to be captured but allows us to hear what 
top of mind for these individuals.  Additionally, it helps to build early relationships and impressions that

Stakeholder Identification:
Depending on the role, it may be impractical to talk to all individuals in the organization.  Therefore, we 
must collaborate with our project contacts who must in turn collaborate with others in the organization 
to identify the key individuals to be interviewed, based upon factors such as seniority, knowledge, and 
communication skills.  Identifying a stakeholder that can speak to multiple areas can lead to time 
efficiencies.  
It is often beneficial to interview several individuals in small groups to avoid redundancy and save time 
during the process.  We should typically avoid interview meetings with large groups of unrelated 
individuals though.  The larger the group setting, the less likely some individuals will be to provide 
insights, while others may be more likely to posture or overstate certain aspects.  
Additional Site Inclusion:
Even if the scope of the project is limited to one site in a multi -site corporation, consideration should be 
given to visiting / interviewing other sites to ensure that a global solution is defined, rather than one 
that only meets the needs of the site in question.  
Agenda Formulation:
We want to be as minimally disruptive as possible to the day -to-day jobs of the individuals we identify to 
interview.  Therefore, sessions should be scheduled based on availability and kept as short as possible.  
Typically 1 -2 hours is the maximum amount of time that can be expected for a specific stakeholder / 
stakeholder group interview session.  
A typical DxDiscovery stakeholder interview agenda for a specific manufacturing site is around 2 -3 days 
in duration.  The following document reference contains a sample agenda:
Sample DxDiscovery Agenda_Questions.xlsx
Our customer project contact should be able to look at calendars and help find specific times during 
which specific stakeholder groups are available.  
The above document reference also contains sample interview questions for each stakeholder group 
that can be tailored based on the customer, industry, and other factors, and included in the meeting 
invites.  
Meeting Invites:
We do not want customer stakeholders to feel like they need to perform a large degree of preparation 
prior to the interview sessions.  However, it is useful to include sample interview questions in the 
invites, along with any other specific requests.  For example, we may want a participant to demonstrate 
a legacy system, bring log sheets or work instruction samples, or perform other prework.  This prework 
should be clearly stated in the invites so time is not wasted obtaining this information during the session 
or waiting for follow -ups to be performed.

Given a text document that is potentially relevant to this activity and a list of entity types, identify all entities of those types from the text and all relationships among the identified entities.
Use en as output language.

---Steps---
1. Identify all entities. For each identified entity, extract the following information:
- entity_name: Name of the entity, use same language as input text. If English, capitalized the name.
- entity_type: One of the following types: [organization,person,geo,event,category]
- entity_description: Comprehensive description of the entity's attributes and activities
Format each entity as ("entity"<|><entity_name><|><entity_type><|><entity_description>)

2. From the entities identified in step 1, identify all pairs of (source_entity, target_entity) that are *clearly related* to each other.
For each pair of related entities, extract the following information:
- source_entity: name of the source entity, as identified in step 1
- target_entity: name of the target entity, as identified in step 1
- relationship_description: explanation as to why you think the source entity and the target entity are related to each other
- relationship_strength: a numeric score indicating strength of the relationship between the source entity and target entity
- relationship_keywords: one or more high-level key words that summarize the overarching nature of the relationship, focusing on concepts or themes rather than specific details
Format each relationship as ("relationship"<|><source_entity><|><target_entity><|><relationship_description><|><relationship_keywords><|><relationship_strength>)

3. Identify high-level key words that summarize the main concepts, themes, or topics of the entire text. These should capture the overarching ideas present in the document.
Format the content-level key words as ("content_keywords"<|><high_level_keywords>)

4. Return output in en as a single list of all the entities and relationships identified in steps 1 and 2. Use **##** as the list delimiter.

5. When finished, output <|COMPLETE|>

The RASCI model specifies definition of stakeholders as follows:
Responsible for ensuring completion of the activity.  The responsible person is the one who does 
the work to complete the task or create the deliverable.  Typically, a RoviSys resource is named as 
responsible for the completion of the various Assessment deliverables, although the customer 
may be responsible for providing prerequisite information.  -
Accountable for reviewing and confirming the completion of the activity.  The accountable party 
approves the deliverable provided as a result of a given assessment activity.  
Typically, a customer resource is named as the accountable party, ensuring the provided 
deliverable is accurate and soliciting feedback from other consulted parties.  Rather than 
requiring the document be signed off by many reviewers, one accountable party helped to 
streamline review and approval cycles.  ○
In the case of stakeholder interview RACI items, the accountable party may be the 
representative providing input during the interview session, but may be required to solicit 
input from other consulted individuals who are not physically present in the session.○
Not every customer stakeholder may be required to review the assessment in its entirety.  A 
production manager may desire to review business process scenarios specific to their area, ○-(Published) MES RIS 102.1 -DxArchitecture RACI

production manager may desire to review business process scenarios specific to their area, 
but need not review the technical architecture envisioned for example.  
Supporting roles may be other RoviSys engineers or individuals assisting the responsible party in 
completing the task at hand in the case of deliverables provided by RoviSys (such as 
documentation).  This may include other RoviSys engineers / functional architects.    -
Consulted during information gathering or deliverable review.  Consulted individuals may be 
additional customer reviewers or individuals from which information is captured by the 
accountable party.    -
Informed throughout the activity, but not required for review or information gathering purposes.  
These individuals are typically customer roles who need to be kept abreast of the progress of the 
activity by being provided status updates, or being included in status update meetings.  They 
might include heads or directors of affected customer teams and senior customer leadership.-
The RoviSys templatized assessment agenda and RACI template will both contain generic stakeholder 
roles.  Translating these generic roles into specific roles possessed by an organization is crucial for 
operational efficiency. Generic roles, while useful for defining broad responsibilities, may not align 
perfectly with the unique structure, capabilities, and expertise within an organization. By mapping these 
roles to specific positions, it is ensured that tasks are assigned to the most suitable individuals. This 
specificity enhances accountability, as it is clear who is responsible for what, and improves 
communication by aligning expectations with actual job functions within the organization. Moreover, it 
allows for more accurate resource planning and utilization, reduces redundancy, and helps in identifying 
any gaps in coverage.  
As a result, RoviSys should discuss with the customer project manager and relevant project team 
members to ensure that the generic roles for which communication is requested is translated to the 
specific roles and responsibilities within the customer's organization while working to identify the key 
individuals for which involvement is requested, rather than simply pass the generic templates to the 
customer and ask for these to be filled in.

constraints that may need to be considered when performing technology selection activities.

Methodology:
The MES division has adopted the 'SIPOC' methodology for the definition of business process scenarios.  
This is an industry standard methodology that has been adapted to better serve the needs of our MES 
project initiatives.  
S = Process suppliers
I = Process inputs
P = Process
O = Process outputs
C = Process consumers
The anatomy of a SIPOC includes the following:
Header: A short description of the activity (business process scenario) being represented by the SIPOC(Published) MES RIS 102.4 -Business Process Scenario 
Definition (SIPOC)
Tuesday, January 9, 2024 8:53 AM

Header: A short description of the activity (business process scenario) being represented by the SIPOC
Inputs: A table containing all envisioned inputs to the process.  This table contains three columns, 
including the following:
Type = a categorization indicating the type of input.  Valid types include:
User○
System○-
Supplier = the user or system role expected to provide the input-
Input Detail = A description of the input itself-
Process: A table outlining the various steps required to execute the process.  This table contains three 
columns, including the following:
Who = a reference to the actor performing the process step.  An actor may be a user or a specific 
system-
What = a description of the process step-
External = A flag indicating that a supporting process step must occur that is envisioned to live 
outside the scope of the system (typically MES solution) being implemented-
Outputs: A table containing all envisioned outputs of the process.  This table contains three columns, 
including the following:
Type = a categorization indicating the type of output.  Valid types include user and system-
Consumer = the recipient of the output.  The consumer will typically leverage the output as an 
input to a subsequent activity-
Output Detail = A description of the output itself-
It is important that SIPOCs be hierarchical in nature, and support drill -down into more specific activities.  
The highest -level SIPOC in a manufacturing facility represents the overall conversion of raw materials as 
input to finished goods as output.  Various sub -processes needed to facilitate this, such as scheduling, 
raw material receiving, quality control, warehousing, etc. all derive from this highest -level SIPOC in some 
manner.  SIPOCs must also be able to be chained together, as the outputs of a given SIPOC are often 
inputs to another.  An example of the hierarchical nature of SIPOCs is shown in the following diagram:
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 46    
Other guidelines concerning the definition of each SIPOC include the following:
The inputs and outputs should capture any person or system that interacts with the MES for the 
scenario-
The process should include all inputs and outputs captured, in addition to any MES operators 
involved directly in the process-
The process should be captured in a way that is clearly the basis for a series of User Stories.  Each 
process step in the lowest -level SIPOC diagrams are likely individual user stories.  
Any inputs / outputs that are of type User would require a UI component.  ○

would be portrayed on the architecture diagram○-

Please Reference:
Usage of SIPOC to Capture Decision Points
Background:
A key consideration when documenting business process scenarios is to properly distill decision points 
throughout the process leveraging the SIPOC format, including all inputs needed to support the decision, 
the process entailed in making the decision, and resulting decision output.  
This is particularly applicable to life sciences digitalization deployments, as the primary driver for the 
initiative is ultimately to support product release by exception.  This necessitates exception scenarios / 
anomalies to be identified and resolved throughout the process, then reviewed subsequent to making a 
final decision concerning the ability of the product to be released to the consumer.  However, a goal of 
digitalization in general is to enable decision makers, and thus it is important for these decision points to 
be properly distilled and agreed upon as part of business process scenario definition.  
Longer -term, if these decision points are properly captured and clearly defined, agentic systems may be 
applied to support decision making, reducing human intervention.  These systems can determine 
specifically when human feedback is required, present targeted information supporting the decision 
making process so that the human need not spend time mining data from disparate data sources, and 
may ultimately be able to make certain decisions autonomously.  Therefore, proper documentation of 
all decision points is essential to future support for such agentic systems.  
SIPOC Hierarchy:
Decision points may warrant creation of dedicated child SIPOC diagrams that are related to higher -
level parents.  For example, there may be an overall SIPOC driving product release upon 
production completion.  This SIPOC may be fed by the output of numerous child SIPOCs, 
representing smaller decision points that feed into the overall product release decision.  For 
example, exception scenarios may arise throughout production warranting scrapping a batch, 
reworking an assembly, or moving forward due to the high likelihood that the product will still be 
compliant.  These decisions must be reviewed and determined to be of no risk to product safety 
prior to the distribution of the product to the consumer.  -
Input and Decision Considerations:
The SIPOC author must ensure that all inputs needed to support the decision in question are 
captured.  This may include both immediate data points created in the context of the batch / 
assembly in question, as well as contextual and historical data from other products / batches / 
production runs that may be needed by a person or agent to properly make a decision.  Some 
examples include the following:-
If a dimensional check fails, measuring equipment calibration records may need to be 
consulted to confirm that the measuring device was properly calibrated within the proper 
time thresholds.  The act of reviewing these records and making a decision should be 
captured as part of the SIPOC documentation process, and the decision made (recalibrate 
and retest the part, fail the part, pass the part, etc.) captured as an output.  ○(Published

ROI Guidance Formulation
It is important to provide our customers guidance concerning how the solutions we propose will provide 
a return on investment (ROI).  It is generally beyond our capabilities to calculate the ROI for our 
customers in a vacuum, as we lack specific knowledge on various costs including raw materials, finished 
goods, labor, etc.  However, we can provide guidelines and examples that our customers can leverage, 
allowing them to plug in financial numbers to determine expected ROI. 
Note that ROI calculations are approximations.  We should err on being conservative with our 
estimations so that customer expectations are managed throughout the initiative.    
There are three primary types of ROI that should be considered:
Legacy system infrastructure and maintenance cost reduction-
Tangible ROI-
Calamity avoidance ROI-
These three considerations are broken down in the following sections.
Legacy System Infrastructure and Maintenance:
Often, MES initiatives are justified due to infrastructure and IT support savings.  Some potential 
considerations include the following:
Reduction in licensing and recurring vendor support costs due to legacy application elimination or 
consolidation-
Reduction in physical infrastructure cost due to consolidation of legacy servers, migration to the 
cloud, removal of costly mainframe systems, or transition from thick clients (physical PCs) to web 
or thin clients-
Reduction in IT / OT support staff due to reduction in the application portfolio requiring upkeep 
and troubleshooting-
Removal of unstable systems requiring frequent intervention to keep running-
Elimination of physical interfaces requiring specialized network hardware, wiring, etc. -
Tangible ROI:
Tangible ROI is based upon direct cost savings due to implementation of new processes enabled by the 
MES platform.  Note that installing the MES platform itself does not provide a tangible ROI.  Rather, the 
efficiencies gained by the new work processes facilitated by the MES are what provide the benefit.  
Therefore, it is important to properly define and manage these work process changes alongside the 
deployment of the MES itself.  
Some examples of tangible ROI include the following:
Reduction in time spent inputting data into the system or running reports to find insights.-
Direct interfaces to external systems such as ERP allowing data to be transferred in real -time 
rather than relying upon manual data transposition-

Optimization algorithms allowing greater throughput due to shop floor schedule optimization and 
resulting increased capacity-

Reduction in safety stock, in -flight WIP, or raw material inventory, in turn increasing working

Standardization of processes, reducing site -or area -specific training demands and ensuring all

Some aspects of tangible ROI may have a greater impact than others, depending on the customer, 
industry, and even region where the plant is located.  Reduction of manual processes may have a

Engagement of the plant financial team is crucial during the ROI formulation exercise to ensure factors

Resource -Based Quotation Methodology
In some cases, a rough schedule and a listing of desired scope items may exist, but there is not enough 
task granularity to formulate a task -based quotation.  It may not be feasible to generate all the various 
tasks due to lack of clarity and/or lack of time.  In these cases, a strategy to give the customer an 
approximate budgetary estimate is to formulate a quotation based upon resource loading. 
Even if a task -based estimate is being created, formulation of a resource -based model can be a useful

one considers the full team that will be required to support the project over the course of the project's 
lifecycle.  A resource -based model may highlight areas that need to be bolstered.  
To formulate this style of quotation, first the calendar schedule is laid out (often within an Excel sheet).  
Calendar time may be represented generically (month one, month two, etc.) if the start date is unclear, 
or a starting date established and the calendar built upon this.

the current sprint.  However, in the event of this overlap, sufficient architect and lead -level 
resources must be available to drive both the current and next sprint.  ○

sequential manner with no overlap.  However, consideration must be given in this scenario 
to ensure that the project developers have value -add tasks during user story development.

Given a text document that is potentially relevant to this activity and a list of entity types, identify all entities of those types from the text and all relationships among the identified entities.
Use en as output language.

---Steps---
1. Identify all entities. For each identified entity, extract the following information:
- entity_name: Name of the entity, use same language as input text. If English, capitalized the name.
- entity_type: One of the following types: [organization,person,geo,event,category]
- entity_description: Comprehensive description of the entity's attributes and activities

2. From the entities identified in step 1, identify all pairs of (source_entity, target_entity) that are *clearly related* to each other.

- target_entity: name of the target entity, as identified in step 1

- relationship_strength: a numeric score indicating strength of the relationship between the source entity and target entity

Execution:

addressed.3.

The executive summary presentation distills the activities, key findings, and recommendations into a 
format that can be digested by broader customer stakeholders including an executive leadership team 
or steering committee.  It should present a compelling plan that highlights the benefits of the initiative, 
roadmap, and keys to success.  
Presentation Components:
The following are the topics typical of an executive summary presentation
Agenda:
The agenda should be presented at the beginning of the presentation so that the group at hand 
understands what will be covered during the discussion.  
Introduction:
Key RoviSys assessment team members, their roles, and credentials should be captured and presented.  
RoviSys Background:
Customer stakeholders unfamiliar with RoviSys will likely benefit from a brief overview of our size, 
locations, and capabilities.  This introduction should be quick and to the point, allowing for ample time 
to cover the logistics and findings within the assessment itself.  
DxArchitecture Activity Overview:
This section should present an overview of the assessment activities and overall timeline involved.
Key Individuals and Sites:

and approved various aspects of the assessment findings.  In the case of a global enterprise -centric 
assessment, the representative site(s) of focus and reasons for selection of those sites as focuses should 
be discussed.  
Capabilities of Focus:

the foundation for the focus of the assessment, including functional capabilities in scope and out of 
scope.  
Key Findings:

including gaps, concerns, and challenges pertaining to current operational workflows.

Overview
Every project we undertake is influenced by whether the customer has purchased a prior Assessment package. This 
document is designed to guide the implementation team when the customer has not purchased a formal Assessment 
engagement and is beginning the project following our Smart Manufacturing Delivery process. Certain components of 
our DxDiscovery and DxArchitecture services offerings must be completed at the project's start as a part of Smart 
Manufacturing Delivery. This additional work should have been included in the proposal, but even if it was not, the 
effort must be accounted for to yield project success.  It is also possible that the customer purchased aspects of the 
DxDiscovery and/or DxArchitecture offerings, but gaps exist that must be completed as part of project implementation.  
Gap Analysis
The following sections review each deliverable from the DxDiscovery and DxArchitecture offerings constituting the 
Assessment package to indicate whether it is applicable. This document serves as a guideline. The Project Manager is 
responsible for ensuring successful project delivery and for determining which features and deliverables from the 
Assessment package should be applied, and to what extent, if the full Assessment package was not purchased prior to 
the engagement.  
Miscellaneous Artifacts
MES RIS 101.1 -Assessment Quotation
This is not applicable. The quote has already been submitted and accepted by the customer. 
DxDiscovery Features

it is the responsibility of the Project Manager to create one. For detailed guidance, please reference MES RAP 
101.2. This ensures that roles and responsibilities are clearly defined and understood, facilitating smooth project 
execution.

current state / constraints and any infrastructure -related consultation required to support the desired end -state 
solution to be able to build the quote. Therefore, it is the responsibility of the Technical Lead to review the 
Infrastructure Evaluation and to fill in any details relevant to the implementation of our commissioned scope.
MES RIS 101.4 -Legacy System Review

current plant processes, constraints, and potential opportunities for replacement or enhancement. While a full 
assessment typically involves an in -depth analysis to deliver robust recommendations, in cases where an 
assessment is not included, a high -level review should be conducted instead. This review focuses on 
understanding the legacy system's capabilities and how they compare to the system being implemented.

Use en as output language.

---Steps---

- entity_description: Comprehensive description of the entity's attributes and activities

DxSustainment
The goal of the DxSustainment effort is to ensure that the customer's technology investment remains 
healthy and viable.  A solution that is out -of-date, hard to support, buggy, or slow -performing will be 
poorly received by the system's user base, and is more likely to be poorly used or abandoned.  The 
DxSustainment effort applies both to systems implemented and deployed by RoviSys and systems 
deployed by others.  In the latter case, the customer may have become frustrated by the previous 
vendor's lack of ongoing support and reached out to RoviSys to help salvage the system so that the 
customer can recoup their technology investment.  
In the case of a system installed by RoviSys, we may be able to draw upon the experience of the project 
team who implemented the system, as well as archived source code, configuration, and documentation.  
In the case of a system installed by others, we will need to quickly triage the system state.  In both cases, 
detailed planning and execution of the sustainment strategy is key to resolving ongoing issues and 
ensuring proactive steps are taken to maintain system value.  
The following features are captured as part of our DxSustainment productized services offering:
System Evaluation:
The system evaluation effort allows the team to gather information concerning the system that will be 
leveraged to formulate a sustainment strategy.  Infrastructure, system versions, log files, server 
resources, and other metrics will be captured and analyzed.  
Knowledge Transfer:
Knowledge transfer allows RoviSys to gain information from various user roles concerning their usage of 
the system, and specific challenges and pain points.  This may include bugs that must be worked around, 
ideas for enhancements, issues accessing the system, and performance concerns.
Additional knowledge transfer may also be required between the current RoviSys project support team 
and new team members who may be brought into the project engagement in a support capability.  This 
includes not only knowledge transfer concerning the system software platform, but also nuances 
concerning the implementation and common support issues.  
Support Desk Establishment:
The support desk provides a means for the customer to submit a support incident (such as an issue or 
enhancement) and provides notification to the support team of this submittal.  The support desk also 
facilitates the ability to track issues and enhancements reported by the customer, including resolution 
status, individual assigned as responsible for the resolution of the support incident, and a trail of 
correspondence that can be consulted should future similar issues arise.

term success and efficiency of the DxSustainment effort. A well -documented repository of system 
configurations, processes, best practices, and troubleshooting guides significantly accelerates 
onboarding for new team members, reducing the learning curve and enabling them to contribute

platform -specific information and assistance.  This Teams instance possesses channels for the common 
MES and digitalization platforms utilized within RoviSys, such as GE, Critical Manufacturing, Parsec 
TrakSYS, and others.  Questions may be posted to these channels concerning best practice, platform 
errors, or how to seek assistance from the vendor.

Root Cause Analysis
Performing a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) for an MES (Manufacturing Execution System) application issue 
requires a structured approach to identifying and resolving the problem effectively. While the specific 
troubleshooting steps depend greatly on the MES platform, data connections, and infrastructure, the 
following are general strategies:
1. Define the Problem Clearly
Gather details on what the issue is, when it started, who reported it, and how it affects 
operations.•
Categorize the issue (e.g., performance degradation, incorrect data, connectivity issues, UI errors).•
2. Reproduce & Validate the Issue
Check if the issue is consistent or intermittent.•
Identify the affected modules, transactions, or processes.•
Determine whether it occurs in production, test, or both environments.•
3. Collect and Analyze Logs & System Data
Check MES application logs for errors or warnings.•
Review database logs for slow queries, deadlocks, or data inconsistencies.•
Utilize a database query profiling tool (such as SQL Server Profiler) to analyze long -running queries •
Monitor server performance (CPU, memory, disk I/O).•
Examine network logs for latency or packet loss.•
Check browser console logs (for web -based MES systems). •
4. Isolate Contributing Factors
Recent software updates or configuration changes.•
Database schema modifications or incorrect data inputs.•
External system integrations (ERP, SCADA, IoT).•
User actions that may trigger the issue.•
System resource constraints or hardware failures.•
5. Use the "5 Whys" or Fishbone Diagram
Apply the 5 Whys method to drill down into the root cause.•
Use a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram to categorize possible causes (software, hardware, network, 
process, user actions).•
6. Test Hypotheses & Validate the Root Cause
Replicate the issue in a controlled test environment.•
Apply temporary fixes (rollback changes, restart services, etc.).•
Use debugging tools to trace errors and bottlenecks.•
7. Implement & Verify the Fix
Deploy a fix in a staging environment before production.•
Ensure that the solution does not create new issues.•
Monitor system behavior post -fix. •(Published) MES RIS 107.10 -Root Cause Analysis

Implement automated monitoring for similar failures.•
Improve error handling & logging.•
Update documentation with RCA findings.•
Train users or update SOPs if needed.•
While MES troubleshooting varies by platform, infrastructure, and integrations, these general strategies 
provide a structured approach to identifying and resolving issues efficiently.
Usage of 5 Whys Strategy:
The 5 Whys is a root cause analysis (RCA) technique used to identify the underlying cause of a problem 
by repeatedly asking "Why?" until the fundamental issue is uncovered. It was developed as part of 
Toyota's Lean Manufacturing System but is widely used in other areas, including MES troubleshooting.
How to Perform the 5 Whys Analysis (example):
State the Problem Clearly
Example: "Production reports in the MES are showing incorrect data."○1.
Ask ‘Why?’ (First Level)
Why is the production report incorrect?
→ Because the MES is pulling incorrect values from the database.○2.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Second Level)
Why is the MES pulling incorrect values?
→ Because the database has duplicate and outdated records.○3.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Third Level)
Why does the database have duplicate and outdated records?
→ Because the data synchronization process failed.○4.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Fourth Level)
Why did the data synchronization process fail?
→ Because a scheduled job responsible for syncing data was not executed.○5.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Fifth Level -Root Cause)
Why was the scheduled job not executed?
→ Because the job scheduler crashed

Even minor enhancements carry some level of risk, making risk assessment a crucial step before

In many cases, a customer may be unfamiliar with the capabilities provided by an MES or MOM 
application, and there may be confusion as to the scope of the initiative as a result.  Even customers 
familiar with the digitalization of operations management functions may lack a deep understanding of 
capabilities provided by the different layers in the ISA -95 model, considering such systems as ERP, 
MES/MOM, SCADA, etc.  During this activity, RoviSys provides an overview of the capabilities provided 
as part of a digitalized ISA -95 compliant solution stack, focusing particularly on Level 3 capabilities most 
often provided by Layer 3 applications.  
Current Process State Definition:
This effort helps to baseline the current state of the facility or facilities under the scope of the 
assessment.  This exercise gives RoviSys background concerning current shop floor activities and system -
level processes that will help to frame the rest of the assessment effort.  
Stakeholder Group Interview Process:
During this activity, RoviSys learns more from key personnel in the enterprise about the processes and 
activities observed during current state process definition.  Probing questions are asked that allows 
RoviSys to draw conclusions concerning what processes work well and what processes could be 
enhanced by a greater degree of digitalization.  
Perceived Benefit: (Next Steps Value Identification)
During this activity, the perceived benefit of pursuing a next step is documented and a justification 
formulated.  While a formal ROI analysis is not typically conducted at this stage, distillment of the 
benefits of moving forward will aid the customer in justifying a larger initiative and provide the customer 
a more specific focus for constrained budgets and resources.  For example, RoviSys may recommend a 
DxArchitecture engagement, DxLean engagement, pilot DxExecution project, or a combination of all 
these productized services offerings. 
Executive Summary:
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 9    
Executive Summary:
The executive summary presentation distills the activities, key findings, and recommendations into a 
format that can be digested by broader customer stakeholders including an executive leadership team 
or steering committee.  It should present a compelling plan that highlights the benefits of moving 
forward with a deeper effort and keys to success.  
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 10    
Please reference: 
DxDiscovery -Quotation.aspx
A proposal must be formulated for the customer that provides the execution strategy for the 
DxDiscovery effort, as well as a cost estimate.  Often, discovery is done as the initial phase in an 
assessment, requiring the assessment package to be quoted in its entirety, but a customer needing high -
level direction with minimal cost impact may choose to execute a DxDiscovery effort in a standalone 
manner.  
RoviSys may be inclined to perform the discovery scope as a cost of sales activity.  However, 
DxDiscovery execution is not only an income stream for RoviSys, but also shows commitment on the 
part of the customer.  The customer is more likely to commit time and resources to the effort if their 
money is on the line.  
Key aspects of interest to the customer that should be detailed within the DxDiscovery proposal include 
the following:
RoviSys background, why are we well suited to perform the activity?  This includes a focus on our 
process overview, digitalization delivery centers of excellence (CoEs), and example success stories•
What are the goals of the DxDiscovery effort?  For example, the customer may be looking to 
replace legacy systems, improve efficiency/quality/etc., support a greenfield plant expansion, 
reduce labor costs, or a host of other 'levers' that can be pulled via usage of digitalization•
Schedule -what activities are envisioned and what is the general duration of each.  •
Deliverables -what is provided to the customer as collateral at the conclusion of the DxDiscovery 
effort?•
RoviSys team -what roles from RoviSys will be supporting the DxDiscovery effort? •
Customer time considerations -what information will be needed from the customer?  Who is 
expected to participate on behalf of the customer and what time commitments will be required of 
these individuals?•
Pricing -What will the DxDiscovery effort cost, including services as well as travel & living 
expenses•
Assumptions -Clarifications concerning assumptions for the DxDiscovery effort •
Typical deliverables provided to the customer as part of the DxDiscovery effort include the following:
Any stakeholder interview recordings captured, as well as sanitized stakeholder interview notes 
captured by RoviSys•
Process background description or corresponding 'current state' SIPOC register•
Legacy system review notes and legacy application register (as applicable)•
Perceived benefit of moving forward with a broader effort, and the direction in which RoviSys 
feels the customer should move forward based upon our findings.  •
Execution summary•
Typical assumptions provided

as part of a digitalized ISA -95 compliant solution stack, focusing particularly on Level 3 capabilities most 
often provided by Layer 3 applications.

following link:
RoviSys S95 capability example.pptx

the various levels.  The focus of a digitalization assessment is largely on Level 3, although other RoviSys 
services as a product (SaaP) offerings may also cover levels 1 & 2.  
Using the generic RoviSys capability map as a guideline, the following associated exercises can be 
conducted with the customer:  
The customer can be educated as to the core capabilities typically provided by a digitalization 
stack, specifically Level 3 operations management capabilities relevant to the assessment effort.

SCADA, ERP, and MES can also be resolved during this review.  -

solution.  There is some risk in providing a demo to the customer that the demo environment will not 
look and feel like the customer's operation, causing confusion or loss of interest.  As a result, RoviSys

Stakeholder Group Interview Process
Purpose:
The stakeholder interview process is important to gain insights facilitating formulation of the 'to -be' 
business process scenarios.  The goal of this exercise is to better understand the role of each 
stakeholder in the manufacturing process, then apply our knowledge of digitalization / MES to 
recommend altered work processes that are likely to provide tangible benefits.  The goal of the exercise 
is NOT for the stakeholder to tell us what those future processes should be.  Stakeholders may have 
opinions concerning various aspects of their daily work, data they wish was more accessible, systems 
that they wish had better user interfaces, etc., and it is important to capture that feedback.  However,  
stakeholders often will not realize that there is a better way to do what they are doing, and the 
customer is paying RoviSys to help identify those insights as part of the assessment.  
The stakeholder group interviews should minimize the time required of both the stakeholders and 
ourselves.  Therefore, these interviews must be properly planned, efficiently executed, and effectively 
documented.  
Current Process State Background:
Ideally, preliminary conversations with the customer project team concerning the goals of the initiative, 
the workflows within the organization, and various plant personnel should provide sufficient 
background to give us an understanding of who we want to talk to and what we want to find out more 
about.  Use this exercise to formulate the scope of the stakeholder interviews.  The size and scope of the 
assessment effort will also come into play.  For example, if we are focusing on a maintenance initiative 
in a certain area it may not be as worthwhile to talk to quality personnel in an unrelated area.

Business Process Scenario Definition:
Business process scenarios capture high level details concerning the various activities (processes) 
envisioned to be executed within the manufacturing enterprise, once digitalization is applied.  Key 
aspects of business process scenario definition include documentation of the specific process steps, as 
well as identification of the specific inputs to the process (incoming data), suppliers of the inputs, 
outputs from the process (outbound data), and consumers of that data.   
Generic Architecture Formulation:
The generic architecture shows the various interactions envisioned between systems as well as 
touchpoints between people and systems (clients, scanners, instruments, etc.), agnostic of a specific 
digitalization platform.  This documentation aids in understanding how the MES/MOM platform stack 
will fit into the overall enterprise systems landscape, and can help better visualize architectural 
constraints that may need to be considered when performing technology selection activities.

Purpose:
Business process scenarios capture high level details concerning the various activities (processes)

The goals of the defined business process scenarios include the following:
Be easily understood by non -technical stakeholders -
Be documented in an efficient, repeatable manner as part of the assessment process-

Highlight required user -to-system and system -to-system interactions, which can be leveraged 
when building more detailed technical documentation (architecture diagrams, value stream maps, 
etc.)-
The functionality basis established by the business process scenarios assists not only with up -front 
understanding of the scope of the solution and value to be provided, but also serves as a basis for future 
implementation and deployment activities.  For example, properly -defined business process scenarios 
can serve as a foundation for testing plans (integration testing, FAT, UAT, etc.) and creation of role -

The MES division has adopted the 'SIPOC' methodology for the definition of business process scenarios.  
This is an industry standard methodology that has been adapted to better serve the needs of our MES 
project initiatives.  
S = Process suppliers
I = Process inputs
P = Process
O = Process outputs
C = Process consumers
The anatomy of a SIPOC includes the following:
Header: A short description of the activity (business process scenario) being represented by the SIPOC(Published) MES RIS 102.4 -Business Process Scenario 
Definition (SIPOC)
Tuesday, January 9, 2024 8:53 AM
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 45    
Header: A short description of the activity (business process scenario) being represented by the SIPOC
Inputs: A table containing all envisioned inputs to the process.  This table contains three columns, 
including the following:
Type = a categorization indicating the type of input.  Valid types include:
User○
System○-
Supplier = the user or system role expected to provide the input-
Input Detail = A description of the input itself-
Process: A table outlining the various steps required to execute the process.  This table contains three 
columns, including the following:
Who = a reference to the actor performing the process step.  An actor may be a user or a specific 
system-
What = a description of the process step-
External = A flag indicating that a supporting process step must occur that is envisioned to live 
outside the scope of the system (typically MES solution) being implemented-
Outputs: A table containing all envisioned outputs of the process.  This table contains three columns, 
including the following:
Type = a categorization indicating the type of output.  Valid types include user and system-
Consumer = the recipient of the output.  The consumer will typically leverage the output as an 
input to a subsequent activity-
Output Detail = A description of the output itself-
It is important that SIPOCs be hierarchical in nature, and support drill -down into more specific activities.  
The highest -level SIPOC in a manufacturing facility represents the overall conversion of raw materials as 
input to finished goods as output.  Various sub -processes needed to facilitate this, such as scheduling, 
raw material receiving, quality control, warehousing, etc. all derive from this highest -level SIPOC in some 
manner.  SIPOCs must also be able to be chained together, as the outputs of a given SIPOC are often 
inputs to another.  An example of the hierarchical nature of SIPOCs is shown in the following diagram:
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 46    
Other guidelines concerning the definition of each SIPOC include the following:
The inputs and outputs should capture any person or system that interacts with the MES for the 
scenario-
The process should include all inputs and outputs captured, in addition to any MES operators 
involved directly in the process-
The process should be captured in a way that is clearly the basis for a series of User Stories.  Each 
process step in the lowest -level SIPOC diagrams are likely individual user stories.  
Any inputs / outputs that are of type User would require a UI component.  ○
Any inputs / outputs that are of type System would require some interface to the MES that 
would be portrayed on the architecture diagram○-
SIPOC Authoring
A preferred template has been created to facilitate SIPOC definition.  Other authoring tools may also be 
appropriate for a specific situation, but the preferred template is recommended as a starting point.  
The preferred template makes use of Microsoft PowerPoint.  This template provides a means of defining 
the SIPOC title, process steps, inputs, and outputs.  Additionally, a PowerPoint link can be added to a 
process step, allowing that step to link to a child SIPOC diagram.  This allows for support of hierarchical 
'drill -down' capabilities.  
At the bottom of a SIPOC diagram, a placeholder allows a reference to a parent SIPOC to be defined.  
This allows 'roll -up' capabilities, so that the viewer can quickly navigate to the parent of a specific SIPOC.  
Lastly, related SIPOCs can be grouped using PowerPoint sections.  
The SIPOC template can be found in the following location:
DxArchitecture SIPOC Template.pptx
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 47    
Examples of SIPOC diagrams can be found in the following locations:
DxArchitecture SIPOC Template -Batch Execution Example.pptx
DxArchitecture SIPOC Template -Customer -specific example.pptx

Usage of SIPOC to Capture Decision Points
Background:
A key consideration when documenting business process scenarios is to properly distill decision points 
throughout the process leveraging the SIPOC format, including all inputs needed to support the decision, 
the process entailed in making the decision, and resulting decision output.  
This is particularly applicable to life sciences digitalization deployments, as the primary driver for the 
initiative is ultimately to support product release by exception.  This necessitates exception scenarios / 
anomalies to be identified and resolved throughout the process, then reviewed subsequent to making a 
final decision concerning the ability of the product to be released to the consumer.  However, a goal of 
digitalization in general is to enable decision makers, and thus it is important for these decision points to 
be properly distilled and agreed upon as part of business process scenario definition.  
Longer -term, if these decision points are properly captured and clearly defined, agentic systems may be 
applied to support decision making, reducing human intervention.  These systems can determine 
specifically when human feedback is required, present targeted information supporting the decision 
making process so that the human need not spend time mining data from disparate data sources, and 
may ultimately be able to make certain decisions autonomously.  Therefore, proper documentation of 
all decision points is essential to future support for such agentic systems.  
SIPOC Hierarchy:
Decision points may warrant creation of dedicated child SIPOC diagrams that are related to higher -
level parents.  For example, there may be an overall SIPOC driving product release upon 
production completion.  This SIPOC may be fed by the output of numerous child SIPOCs, 
representing smaller decision points that feed into the overall product release decision.  For 
example, exception scenarios may arise throughout production warranting scrapping a batch, 
reworking an assembly, or moving forward due to the high likelihood that the product will still be 
compliant.  These decisions must be reviewed and determined to be of no risk to product safety 
prior to the distribution of the product to the consumer.  -
Input and Decision Considerations:
The SIPOC author must ensure that all inputs needed to support the decision in question are 
captured.  This may include both immediate data points created in the context of the batch / 
assembly in question, as well as contextual and historical data from other products / batches / 
production runs that may be needed by a person or agent to properly make a decision.  Some 
examples include the following:-
If a dimensional check fails, measuring equipment calibration records may need to be 
consulted to confirm that the measuring device was properly calibrated within the proper 
time thresholds.  The act of reviewing these records and making a decision should be 
captured as part of the SIPOC documentation process, and the decision made (recalibrate 
and retest the part, fail the part, pass the part, etc.) captured as an output.  ○(Published

Generic Architecture
The generic architecture shows the various interactions envisioned between systems as well as 
touchpoints between people and systems (clients, scanners, instruments, etc.), agnostic of a specific 
digitalization platform.  This documentation aids in understanding how the MES/MOM platform stack 
will fit into the overall enterprise systems landscape, and can help better visualize architectural 
constraints that may need to be considered when performing technology selection activities.  
There are two common processes leveraged to document a generic architecture.  One or both of these 
may be of use to generate and provide to the customer during the assessment phase.  
Block Diagram:
A block diagram shows specific systems or system placeholders and associated interconnections 
between them.  The block diagram is often organized according to the ISA -95 hierarchy:
ERP-
MES / MOM-
SCADA / HMI-
Controls-
Legacy systems and applications expected to remain within the solution stack can be explicitly called 
out, while placeholders for new applications can be referenced generically.  Additionally, it can be useful 
to document 'before and after' block diagrams

other aspects related to infrastructure (like user interface types and locations).

highlight cases where the architecture envisioned is overly complex.  For example, a large number of 
crisscrossed point -to-point interfaces could be replaced by a centralized data pipeline / universal

The result of the technology selection activity is clarity concerning the solution stack that will be 
leveraged to deliver on the envisioned process scenarios and corresponding ROI.  A variety of

selection(s) made.  
Technology Platform Shortlist:
The first step in executing the technology assessment is shortlisting the platforms to be evaluated.  If 
RoviSys was contracted directly by the customer to perform an independent analysis, we have the 
opportunity to select and rate various competing platform solutions.  However, if RoviSys was brought 
into the opportunity by a vendor, we may not be afforded this opportunity.  In this case, the technology 
assessment should focus on how to best utilize the vendor platform and where weaknesses in the 
vendor platform may require supplemental components that RoviSys can recommend due to our 
independence.  
Given the hundreds of platforms and niche solutions on the market, it is impractical to evaluate every 
option.  Rather, our experience is applied to first recommend a set of short -listed candidates.  Typically,

MES priority platforms that we feel may have merit as the basis for the solution.  This is based

scenarios.  However, an extremely cost -conscious customer may weight cost more heavily than user 
experience fit.  External system integration may not be as important to a customer with a limited 
external solution stack.

It is important to provide our customers guidance concerning how the solutions we propose will provide 
a return on investment (ROI).  It is generally beyond our capabilities to calculate the ROI for our 
customers in a vacuum, as we lack specific knowledge on various costs including raw materials, finished 
goods, labor, etc.  However, we can provide guidelines and examples that our customers can leverage, 
allowing them to plug in financial numbers to determine expected ROI. 
Note that ROI calculations are approximations.  We should err on being conservative with our 
estimations so that customer expectations are managed throughout the initiative.    
There are three primary types of ROI that should be considered:
Legacy system infrastructure and maintenance cost reduction-
Tangible ROI-
Calamity avoidance ROI-
These three considerations are broken down in the following sections.
Legacy System Infrastructure and Maintenance:
Often, MES initiatives are justified due to infrastructure and IT support savings.  Some potential 
considerations include the following:
Reduction in licensing and recurring vendor support costs due to legacy application elimination or 
consolidation-
Reduction in physical infrastructure cost due to consolidation of legacy servers, migration to the 
cloud, removal of costly mainframe systems, or transition from thick clients (physical PCs) to web 
or thin clients-
Reduction in IT / OT support staff due to reduction in the application portfolio requiring upkeep 
and troubleshooting-
Removal of unstable systems requiring frequent intervention to keep running-
Elimination of physical interfaces requiring specialized network hardware, wiring, etc. -
Tangible ROI:
Tangible ROI is based upon direct cost savings due to implementation of new processes enabled by the 
MES platform.  Note that installing the MES platform itself does not provide a tangible ROI.  Rather, the 
efficiencies gained by the new work processes facilitated by the MES are what provide the benefit.  
Therefore, it is important to properly define and manage these work process changes alongside the 
deployment of the MES itself.  
Some examples of tangible ROI include the following:
Reduction in time spent inputting data into the system or running reports to find insights.-
Direct interfaces to external systems such as ERP allowing data to be transferred in real -time 
rather than relying upon manual data transposition-

customer review and approval cycles can occur without overall program disruption, specifically in the 
case where multiple proposals are being 'carved out' as execution throughout a multiple phase initiative 
progresses.  This ensures that project momentum is maintained and the project team can be kept intact.   
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 67    
Please Reference:
Resource -Based Quotation Methodology
In some cases, a rough schedule and a listing of desired scope items may exist, but there is not enough 
task granularity to formulate a task -based quotation.  It may not be feasible to generate all the various 
tasks due to lack of clarity and/or lack of time.  In these cases, a strategy to give the customer an 
approximate budgetary estimate is to formulate a quotation based upon resource loading. 
Even if a task -based estimate is being created, formulation of a resource -based model can be a useful 
'cross -check' to ensure that the task estimates are realistic.  Task -based estimates tend to be light when 
one considers the full team that will be required to support the project over the course of the project's 
lifecycle.  A resource -based model may highlight areas that need to be bolstered.  
To formulate this style of quotation, first the calendar schedule is laid out (often within an Excel sheet).  
Calendar time may be represented generically (month one, month two, etc.) if the start date is unclear, 
or a starting date established and the calendar built upon this.  
Next, the calendar time within the schedule is split up according to envisioned project phases.  Key 
phases that may be represented include the following examples:
Assessment•
Project planning•
User story definition•
Sprint execution (x number of sprints envisioned)•
Sprint testing (x number of sprints envisioned)•
Sprint deployment•
Hypercare support•
The duration of a specific phase is approximated based upon the customer's schedule constraints and 
our experience in the time required to complete given tasks.  The customer may have a target go -live 
date aligned to a site startup, supporting system (such as ERP) cutover, or other factors.  In these cases, 
one can work backward from the go -live date to slot in the various activities above.  
Some timeline approximations are as follows:
A full assessment effort, including site visit, business process scenario definition, technology 
comparison, architecture formulation, roadmap formulation, and executive summary, typically  
requires between 6 and 8 weeks, although this time period can be compressed.  •
Detailed project planning is often a 2 -week effort •
User story definition may typically take between 1 and 2 weeks prior to the kickoff of each sprints
Definition of initial user stories must be done before the commencement of the first sprint.  
Thereafter, user story definition for the next sprint can overlap with execution and testing of 
the current sprint.  However, in the event of this overlap, sufficient architect and lead -level 
resources must be available to drive both the current and next sprint.  ○
There may be a desire to sequence user story development and sprint build/test in a 
sequential manner with no overlap.  However, consideration must be given in this scenario 
to ensure that the project developers have value -add tasks during user story development.  
Otherwise, it is impractical to ramp the development team on and off the project to keep 
them busy during user story definition.  ○•
Sprint execution is often 4 -6 weeks in duration, although this is dependent upon the complexity of 
the sprint.  It is at the estimator's discretion based on project scope and experience whether a 
larger number of shorter sprints (2 weeks for example) or a smaller number of longer sprints are

The process activity diagram documents the various production processes in a 'swim lane' format, showing the 
system responsible for each activity, as well as system -to-system interactions or user -to-system interactions.  This 
activity is especially useful to facilitate a technical team's understanding of the role of various systems and how 
they fit together.  The process activity diagram highlights areas where detailed system interface design will be 
required, as well as cases where user interfaces will need to be made available. This is a valuable exercise to 
complete in order to understand interface constraints on the new system. The Technical Lead is responsible for

SIPOC Definition
Suppliers The entities (people, organizations, or systems) that provide the necessary inputs for the process.
Inputs The resources, materials, or information needed to perform the process.
Process The series of steps or activities carried out to convert inputs into outputs.
Outputs The products, services, or results produced by the process.
Customers The end -users or beneficiaries of the process outputs.
Roles & Responsibilities•
Roles Responsibilities
Scrum Master Facilitates the Scrum process, ensuring the team adheres to Agile principles and practices. 
Removes impediments and fosters collaboration among team members. Prioritizes 
managing the work items in the current sprint.
Product Owner Represents the stakeholders and is responsible for defining the product backlog, 
prioritizing features, and ensuring the team delivers value to the customer. Prioritizes 
preparing work items for future sprints.
Solution Architect Designs the overall system architecture, ensuring that the technical structure aligns with 
the business goals and is scalable, reliable, and maintainable.
Technical Lead Provides technical direction and oversight to the development team, ensuring best 
practices are followed and the technical implementation aligns with the project's goals.
Functional Analyst Analyzes business requirements and translates them into functional specifications for the 
development team, ensuring that the software meets the needs of the users.
Senior 
Developer/EngineerAn experienced developer responsible for implementing complex features, mentoring

What Information is Required in a User Story
To start you need an epic and, in most cases, features. ○
What we include in Features:
Title -A clear, concise title that describes what the feature is about.▪
Description -A brief summary of the feature, explaining its purpose and the problem it solves. You can 
use the SIPOC to answer the following questions if you're having trouble formulating this: 
Objective? □
Who?□
What?□
When?□▪
Definition of Done/Success Criteria ▪
Related Documents▪○
So for example, the CRM23B epic would be "The Implementation of Critical Manufacturing" and the features 
for that project would have been:
PLM ▪
Operator Cockpit ▪
Supplier Integration ▪
SAP▪○
Meaning that every user story that was created can be placed in one of the 4 categories listed above.○•
Utilizing SIPOC
In user story creation you care about suppliers and inputs because of how they affect what you're creating, 
you care about the process because that is essentially the user story, and you care about the outputs and 
customers because that's the end result of your work, and who will be evaluating whether or not the work 
that was done is correct.○
You can read more about SIPOC and how we utilize it here:
MES RIS 101.7 -Business Process Scenario Definition ▪○

ADO Field Definition
Title SIPOC Focus : Process •
This should be a concise summary of the process you are improving or feature you are 
working on. Think about the core process or goal this story targets.•
Description SIPOC Focus : Process & Outputs •
Provide a detailed description of what the user story covers. This should outline the steps 
in the process (from the SIPOC) and describe the expected outputs. Think about how the 
inputs get transformed by the process.•

Define what success looks like from the perspective of the customers in your SIPOC. This 
is where you articulate what needs to be achieved for the outputs to meet customer 
expectations.•

SpecificationsSIPOC Focus : Inputs & Process •
Break down the functional requirements that detail how the process transforms the 
inputs. Functional specifications should specify what technical or business inputs are 
necessary and how they flow through the process.•
Technical Details SIPOC Focus : Inputs & Process •
Highlight the technical inputs and details involved. You might refer to specific systems, 
APIs, or components needed to execute the process.•

Knowledge Transfer
Knowledge transfer may be required in two different scenarios.  In the case of a system that was not 
originally implemented by RoviSys, the knowledge transfer process allows RoviSys to gain information 
from various user roles concerning their usage of the system, and specific challenges and pain points.  
This may include bugs that must be worked around, ideas for enhancements, issues accessing the 
system, and performance concerns.
In the case of a system that was installed by RoviSys, knowledge transfer may be required between the 
current RoviSys project support team and new team members who may be brought into the project 
engagement in a support capability.  This includes not only knowledge transfer concerning the system 
software platform, but also nuances concerning the implementation and common support issues.  
Prior to the Knowledge Transfer Session:
As with system evaluation, creation of a knowledge transfer checklist is important to provide structure 
to the knowledge transfer effort and ensure that it is conducted efficiently.  An initial step in the 
knowledge transfer process is identification of the specific user roles who will participate, particularly in 
the case of knowledge transfer being provided to RoviSys by the customer.  End user roles are most 
adept at how the software functions and how it is utilized on a day -to-day basis.  
It may first be necessary to obtain a customer process overview by a customer SME so that the RoviSys 
team understands the manufacturing process and can put system operations within the context of these 
processes.  
Based upon the system evaluation effort, RoviSys should be able to map out displays and functions of 
focus.  As these are presented by relevant customer SMEs, RoviSys can check off discovered displays / 
functions to ensure that none are missed.  
During the Knowledge Transfer Session:
Leveraging the created checklist, RoviSys personnel can execute a session with each identified customer 
super user to capture how the software is leveraged.  The customer should demonstrate common 
functions, data input, data output, and decisions made leveraging the software.  Any functions with 
which the user struggles or bugs / workarounds captured should be noted.  
An attempt should be made to record these sessions whenever possible so that redundant sessions are 
not required should the RoviSys support team change.  
The RoviSys team should at a minimum consist of a lead who is driving the session and asking prompting 
questions, as well as a designated notetaker.  
Post Knowledge Transfer Session:
Notes should be sanitized, condensed, and made available to the customer for reference / review.  
These notes should also be stored in a shared repository accessible to the broader RoviSys 
DxSustainment team, such as a OneNote notebook.  (Published) MES RIS 107.3 -Knowledge Transfer

A Fishbone Diagram, also known as an Ishikawa Diagram or Cause -and-Effect Diagram, is a tool used to 
identify the root causes of a problem systematically. It allows the troubleshooter to visually maps out 
potential factors contributing to an issue, organizing them into major categories.
Structure of a Fishbone Diagram:
The "head" of the fish represents the problem statement (effect).•
The "spine" is the main horizontal line extending from the head.•
   RAPs for MES -Development Page 134

Software –Bugs, application crashes, configuration errors. 1.

Root Cause Analysis
Performing a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) for an MES (Manufacturing Execution System) application issue 
requires a structured approach to identifying and resolving the problem effectively. While the specific 
troubleshooting steps depend greatly on the MES platform, data connections, and infrastructure, the 
following are general strategies:
1. Define the Problem Clearly
Gather details on what the issue is, when it started, who reported it, and how it affects 
operations.•
Categorize the issue (e.g., performance degradation, incorrect data, connectivity issues, UI errors).•
2. Reproduce & Validate the Issue
Check if the issue is consistent or intermittent.•
Identify the affected modules, transactions, or processes.•
Determine whether it occurs in production, test, or both environments.•
3. Collect and Analyze Logs & System Data
Check MES application logs for errors or warnings.•
Review database logs for slow queries, deadlocks, or data inconsistencies.•
Utilize a database query profiling tool (such as SQL Server Profiler) to analyze long -running queries •
Monitor server performance (CPU, memory, disk I/O).•
Examine network logs for latency or packet loss.•
Check browser console logs (for web -based MES systems). •
4. Isolate Contributing Factors
Recent software updates or configuration changes.•
Database schema modifications or incorrect data inputs.•
External system integrations (ERP, SCADA, IoT).•
User actions that may trigger the issue.•
System resource constraints or hardware failures.•
5. Use the "5 Whys" or Fishbone Diagram
Apply the 5 Whys method to drill down into the root cause.•
Use a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram to categorize possible causes (software, hardware, network, 
process, user actions).•
6. Test Hypotheses & Validate the Root Cause
Replicate the issue in a controlled test environment.•
Apply temporary fixes (rollback changes, restart services, etc.).•
Use debugging tools to trace errors and bottlenecks.•
7. Implement & Verify the Fix
Deploy a fix in a staging environment before production.•
Ensure that the solution does not create new issues.•

Usage of 5 Whys Strategy:
The 5 Whys is a root cause analysis (RCA) technique used to identify the underlying cause of a problem 
by repeatedly asking "Why?" until the fundamental issue is uncovered. It was developed as part of 
Toyota's Lean Manufacturing System but is widely used in other areas, including MES troubleshooting.
How to Perform the 5 Whys Analysis (example):
State the Problem Clearly

Ask ‘Why?’ (First Level)
Why is the production report incorrect?
→ Because the MES is pulling incorrect values from the database.○2.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Second Level)
Why is the MES pulling incorrect values?
→ Because the database has duplicate and outdated records.○3.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Third Level)
Why does the database have duplicate and outdated records?
→ Because the data synchronization process failed.○4.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Fourth Level)
Why did the data synchronization process fail?
→ Because a scheduled job responsible for syncing data was not executed.○5.
Ask ‘Why?’ Again (Fifth Level -Root Cause)
Why was the scheduled job not executed?
→ Because the job scheduler crashed

Given a text document that is potentially relevant to this activity and a list of entity types, identify all entities of those types from the text and all relationships among the identified entities.
Use en as output language.

---Steps---
1. Identify all entities. For each identified entity, extract the following information:
- entity_name: Name of the entity, use same language as input text. If English, capitalized the name.
- entity_type: One of the following types: [organization,person,geo,event,category]
- entity_description: Comprehensive description of the entity's attributes and activities
Format each entity as ("entity"<|><entity_name><|><entity_type><|><entity_description>)

2. From the entities identified in step 1, identify all pairs of (source_entity, target_entity) that are *clearly related* to each other.
For each pair of related entities, extract the following information:
- source_entity: name of the source entity, as identified in step 1
- target_entity: name of the target entity, as identified in step 1
- relationship_description: explanation as to why you think the source entity and the target entity are related to each other
- relationship_strength: a numeric score indicating strength of the relationship between the source entity and target entity
- relationship_keywords: one or more high-level key words that summarize the overarching nature of the relationship, focusing on concepts or themes rather than specific details
Format each relationship as ("relationship"<|><source_entity><|><target_entity><|><relationship_description><|><relationship_keywords><|><relationship_strength>)

3. Identify high-level key words that summarize the main concepts, themes, or topics of the entire text. These should capture the overarching ideas present in the document.

---Goal---
Given a text document that is potentially relevant to this activity and a list of entity types, identify all entities of those types from the text and all relationships among the identified entities.
Use en as output language.

---Steps---
1. Identify all entities. For each identified entity, extract the following information:
- entity_name: Name of the entity, use same language as input text. If English, capitalized the name.
- entity_type: One of the following types: [organization,person,geo,event,category]
- entity_description: Comprehensive description of the entity's attributes and activities
Format each entity as ("entity"<|><entity_name><|><entity_type><|><entity_description>)

2. From the entities identified in step 1, identify all pairs of (source_entity, target_entity) that are *clearly related* to each other.
For each pair of related entities, extract the following information:
- source_entity: name of the source entity, as identified in step 1
- target_entity: name of the target entity, as identified in step 1
- relationship_description: explanation as to why you think the source entity and the target entity are related to each other
- relationship_strength: a numeric score indicating strength of the relationship between the source entity and target entity
- relationship_keywords: one or more high-level key words that summarize the overarching nature of the relationship, focusing on concepts or themes rather than specific details
Format each relationship as ("relationship"<|><source_entity><|><target_entity><|><relationship_description><|><relationship_keywords><|><relationship_strength>)

3. Identify high-level key words that summarize the main concepts, themes, or topics of the entire text. These should capture the overarching ideas present in the document.
